name: Blissful ignorance effect
statement: After committing to a choice, people are said to expect better outcomes from vague information than from precise information, a gap that is smaller before they commit.
meaning: The claim is an interaction, not a preference for knowing less. Two things vary: whether the information given is precise or vague, and whether it arrives before an action or after one. Mishra, Shiv and Nayakankuppam say that vague information produces more optimistic outcome expectancies after an action than before it, and that precise information narrows the difference. Their account rests on two motives borrowed from work on motivated reasoning. Before acting, a person wants to be right, so precision helps. After acting, the person wants the choice to have been good, and vague wording is loose enough to be read that way. Nothing in the claim says a buyer who is told less will enjoy the product more. It says that the same loose wording buys more optimism once the money has been spent.

origin.who: Himanshu Mishra, Baba Shiv and Dhananjay Nayakankuppam
origin.note: The paper names the effect. Its abstract reports three experiments and states that the pattern arises from the interplay of a directional goal, arriving at a desired conclusion, and an accuracy goal.

evidence: What the original paper did could not be read at first hand for this entry. The article sits behind Oxford University Press's paywall, and Unpaywall records it as closed with no repository copy, so no participant counts, condition means, test statistics or effect sizes are quoted here. The abstract, read at the publisher and again at RePEc, says this: across three experiments, individuals given vague information are more optimistic about outcomes post-action than pre-action, and the difference is attenuated with precise information. The abstract does not name the products or the measures. A press release issued by University of Chicago Press Journals on 15 September 2008 says the three experiments had participants making choices about chocolates, hand lotions and animated movies, and that vague information after the decision went with greater optimism than detailed information before it. That description of the designs is at one remove, and figures quoted in later popular summaries, including specific probabilities and percentage gaps, were not found in any document reached for this entry.

replication.headline: No repeat of the three experiments was found, and the paper has been cited about thirty times in eighteen years.
replication.detail: Semantic Scholar lists 30 works citing the 2008 paper and OpenAlex counts 31. Every one of the 30 was read by title and venue. They are applications and reviews in marketing, auditing, sustainability and finance, and none is described as a repeat of the original design. The FORRT Replication Database explorer dataset, 2,164 original-replication pairs when downloaded on 10 August 2026, holds no row for this effect, and neither does its companion FLoRA library of 2,334 annotated entries. A Europe PMC search for 'blissful ignorance' returned 199 records, all of them clinical or editorial uses of the phrase. Crossref searches on the title and on the authors, and general web searches for replication and preregistration terms paired with the effect's name, turned up nothing. OpenAlex was rate-limited before a full citation sweep could be run there. PsycINFO and the Journal of Consumer Research's own citing-article list were not searched.

limits: The evidence for this effect is one paper that this entry could not open. Sample sizes are the obvious gap. Consumer laboratory experiments of that period often ran a few dozen students per cell, and whether these did cannot be settled from the abstract or the press release. No effect size for the interaction is available from any source reached here. The mechanism has been tested elsewhere with mixed results. Mishra, Mishra and Shiv later argued in Psychological Science that vague information boosts performance because people read it the way they wish, reporting two laboratory studies and one quasi-field study on mental acuity, physical strength and weight loss; that abstract gives no participant counts either. Green and van Deemter ran experiments on vague expressions inside referring noun phrases and concluded that the gains attributed to vagueness come from factors that travel with it rather than from vagueness itself. Their materials are linguistic rather than commercial, so the conclusion transfers only as far as the shared mechanism does. Neither paper repeats the pre-action against post-action comparison that defines the blissful ignorance effect.
misreadings: The popular form of this claim is not the published one. Wikipedia's article opens by saying that people with good information about a product are not expected to be as happy with it as people with less information, and cites Schiffman's textbook Consumer Behavior, page 95, for that sentence and Solomon's textbook of the same name, page 318, for a two-group experiment. The article never cites Mishra, Shiv and Nayakankuppam anywhere. Two changes have crept in along the way. Happiness with a product has replaced expectancy about an outcome, and the before-and-after contrast, which is the whole finding, has dropped out, leaving a bare claim that ignorance is pleasant. Three neighbouring ideas are not this one. The ostrich effect is about declining to look at information a person could have for nothing, and has its own entry here. Wilful ignorance is a choice to stay uninformed, usually to avoid a moral or financial obligation, and the blissful ignorance effect involves no such choice: the information is handed to everybody, and only its precision differs. Choice-supportive bias concerns memory of the option's features after the fact, not predictions about how it will turn out. The forecast being distorted here is about a future outcome, which places the claim beside affective forecasting rather than inside it, since affective forecasting concerns how strongly the event will be felt rather than whether it will go well.
